name: RSI bull-range support test (Cardwell/Brown range rules)
rule: r=ctx.rsi(14). bullRange(i) = max(r over bars i-59..i) >= 70 AND min(r over the same bars) >= 35. ENTER long at close of bar i if flat AND bullRange AND r[i-1] < 45 AND r[i] >= 45 AND min(r over bars i-5..i) <= 42. EXIT (flat) when r < 35 (bull range broken) OR r >= 70 (top of the bull range). Long only, full size.
rationale: Cardwell's observation: in uptrends RSI(14) oscillates in a 40-80 range and the 40-50 zone acts as support; buying the bounce off that support trades with the trend instead of fading it like the textbook 30/70 rule.
source: Andrew Cardwell RSI range rules; Constance Brown, Technical Analysis for the Trading Professional (McGraw-Hill 1999), ch.1

name: RSI 60/40 range-shift hysteresis (Cardwell)
rule: r=ctx.rsi(14). ENTER long when r[i-1] <= 60 AND r[i] > 60 (RSI shifts into the bull range). EXIT when r < 40 (shift to the bear range). Long only; otherwise hold the current state.
rationale: A 60/40 band instead of the 50 midline (already tested) adds hysteresis: fewer whipsaws, and the 60 cross confirms a range shift rather than a coin-flip tick above 50.
source: Andrew Cardwell RSI range shifts; Brown (1999) ch.1; popularised on TradingView as 'RSI range filter'

name: RSI failure swing bottom (Wilder 1978)
rule: r=ctx.rsi(14). State machine in ctx.state: phase0: if r < 30 -> trough1 = min r while r<30, start=i. When r crosses back above 30 -> phase1, peak = r. phase1: peak = max(peak, r); if r < peak - 3 -> phase2, trough2 = r. phase2: trough2 = min(trough2, r); if trough2 < trough1 OR i - start > 30 -> reset to phase0; if r > peak (RSI breaks the fail point) -> ENTER long. EXIT when r >= 70 OR r < trough2 OR 20 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Wilder's own RSI signal: a higher RSI trough after an oversold reading plus a break of the intervening RSI peak is momentum confirmation of a price bottom, unlike the raw 30 touch most retail tests use.
source: J. Welles Wilder, New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (1978), pp.63-70 ('failure swings')

name: RSI crosses its own 14-period SMA (TradingView default RSI-based MA)
rule: r=ctx.rsi(14); m = SMA14 of r (ctx.rolling(14) fed once per bar). ENTER long when r[i-1] <= m[i-1] AND r[i] > m[i] AND r[i] > 50. EXIT when r[i] < m[i]. Long only.
rationale: The default TradingView RSI panel draws an SMA(14) on RSI; the cross is the single most-asked 'what does this line mean' question. It is a smoothed momentum-of-momentum cross that lags less than a price MA cross.
source: TradingView built-in 'Relative Strength Index' (MA Type SMA, MA Length 14); https://www.tradingview.com/support/solutions/43000502338-relative-strength-index-rsi/

name: RSI 30 dip only in a ranging market (ADX < 20 gate)
rule: ADX(14) Wilder: TR, +DM, -DM smoothed with RMA alpha=1/14; +DI=100*s(+DM)/s(TR); -DI likewise; DX=100*|+DI - -DI|/(+DI + -DI); ADX = RMA14 of DX. ENTER long when flat AND ADX < 20 AND ctx.rsi(14) < 30. EXIT when rsi > 55 OR ADX > 25 OR 15 bars held. Long only.
rationale: The most repeated 'pro tip' about RSI is that oversold readings only mean-revert in ranges; gating by ADX < 20 is the standard way retail is taught to implement that.
source: Babypips School of Pipsology 'ADX'; Investopedia 'How to use ADX'; Wilder (1978) ADX < 20 = no trend

name: Weekly RSI > 50 trend, daily RSI 40 pullback (multi-timeframe RSI)
rule: W = ctx.resample(bars,'1w') using COMPLETE weeks only; wRSI = Wilder RSI(14) of weekly closes. d = ctx.rsi(14) daily. ENTER long when wRSI > 50 AND d[i-1] < 40 AND d[i] >= 40. EXIT when d > 70 OR wRSI < 50 (checked on the first bar after a week completes). Long only.
rationale: Top-down 'trade with the higher timeframe' is the dominant retail doctrine; a weekly RSI above 50 is the higher-timeframe trend, and the daily RSI 40 reclaim is the low-risk entry inside it.
source: Alexander Elder, Trading for a Living (1993) triple screen principle; Brown (1999) RSI range rules applied across timeframes

name: Hourly RSI 30 reclaim above the 200 EMA (crypto)
rule: ENTER long when close > ctx.ema('close',200) AND ctx.rsi(14) at i-1 < 30 AND ctx.rsi(14) at i >= 30. EXIT when rsi > 60 OR close < EMA200 OR 48 bars held. Long only.
rationale: The most-viewed intraday 'RSI strategy' videos pair an oversold RSI with a 200 EMA trend filter; buying the reclaim (not the dip itself) avoids catching falling knives in a 24/7 market.
source: Widely taught 'RSI + 200 EMA' intraday setup (e.g. YouTube backtest channels 2020-2023); Wilder (1978) RSI

name: MACD zero-line cross (Murphy)
rule: MACD(12,26,9): line = EMA12(close) - EMA26(close) via ctx.ema; signal = EMA9 of line (custom EMA: alpha=2/(n+1), seeded with the first available value); hist = line - signal. ENTER long when line[i-1] <= 0 AND line[i] > 0. EXIT when line < 0. Long only.
rationale: The zero-line cross is the slower, less-noisy MACD signal (EMA12 crossing EMA26) that Murphy recommends over the signal cross; it has never been isolated here from the signal-line version.
source: John J. Murphy, Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (1999), ch.10 MACD

name: MACD signal cross taken only above the zero line
rule: MACD(12,26,9): line = EMA12(close) - EMA26(close) via ctx.ema; signal = EMA9 of line (custom EMA: alpha=2/(n+1), seeded with the first available value); hist = line - signal. ENTER long when line crosses above signal (line[i-1] <= signal[i-1], line[i] > signal[i]) AND line[i] > 0. EXIT when line < signal. Long only.
rationale: The standard 'pro' MACD filter: only bullish crosses that occur with positive momentum (above zero) count, dropping the counter-trend crosses that produce most of the plain cross's losses.
source: Gerald Appel, Technical Analysis: Power Tools for Active Investors (2005), ch.8; common TradingView/Investopedia MACD tweak

name: MACD histogram uptick below zero (Elder)
rule: MACD(12,26,9): line = EMA12(close) - EMA26(close) via ctx.ema; signal = EMA9 of line (custom EMA: alpha=2/(n+1), seeded with the first available value); hist = line - signal. ENTER long when hist[i] < 0 AND hist[i-1] <= hist[i-2] AND hist[i] > hist[i-1] (first uptick after a decline below zero). EXIT when (hist[i] > 0 AND hist[i] < hist[i-1]) OR hist[i] < histAtEntry (new low) OR 20 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Elder argues the histogram's slope change leads the signal-line cross by several bars; the uptick-below-zero entry buys the momentum turn early rather than the lagging cross.
source: Alexander Elder, Trading for a Living (1993), ch.26 MACD-Histogram

name: Raschke 3/10 oscillator first cross
rule: osc = ctx.sma('close',3) - ctx.sma('close',10); sig = SMA16 of osc (ctx.rolling(16)). ENTER long when osc[i-1] <= sig[i-1] AND osc[i] > sig[i]. EXIT when osc < sig. Long only.
rationale: Raschke's 3/10 is a fast MACD built from simple averages; its first cross after a pullback is her core swing-trade timing tool, and it is faster than the 12/26 default most retail tests use.
source: Linda Bradford Raschke & Laurence Connors, Street Smarts (1995); Raschke, LBR Group '3/10 oscillator'

name: Best Six Months with MACD timing (Hirsch)
rule: MACD(12,26,9): line = EMA12(close) - EMA26(close) via ctx.ema; signal = EMA9 of line (custom EMA: alpha=2/(n+1), seeded with the first available value); hist = line - signal. Dates from bar.time in UTC. ENTER long on the first bar on/after 1 Oct where line > signal (keep looking until 30 Apr). EXIT on the first bar on/after 1 May where line < signal (keep looking until 30 Sep). Otherwise hold the current state. Long only. SPY is holdout: QQQ/DIA stand in (proxyFor SPY->QQQ). proxyFor goes in meta.proxyFor; QQQ and DIA are in assets.
rationale: The Almanac's refinement of 'sell in May': use MACD to delay the seasonal entry until momentum turns up and delay the exit until it turns down, which Hirsch claims roughly doubles the plain seasonal result.
source: Jeffrey Hirsch, Stock Trader's Almanac, 'Best Six Months Switching Strategy with MACD Timing' (annual); Sy Harding, Riding the Bear (1999)

name: Bollinger W-bottom (Bollinger's own setup)
rule: mid=ctx.sma('close',20), sd=ctx.rollingStd('close',20), lower=mid-2sd, upper=mid+2sd, pctB=(close-lower)/(upper-lower). phase0: when pctB < 0 -> low1 = close, start=i, phase1. phase1: low1 = min(low1, close) while pctB < 0; when pctB > 0.5 -> neck = close, phase2. phase2: neck = max(neck, close); if close <= low1*1.01 AND pctB > 0 -> low2 = close, phase3. phase3: low2 = min(low2, close); if close < lower -> reset; if close > neck -> ENTER long. Any phase: if i - start > 40 -> reset. EXIT when pctB > 1 OR close < low2 OR 30 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Bollinger's W-bottom is a double bottom where the second low holds inside the band while price is as low or lower: relative strength on the retest, confirmed by a neckline break. It is the setup he says the bands were built to identify.
source: John Bollinger, Bollinger on Bollinger Bands (2001), ch.15 'W-bottoms'

name: Bollinger lower-band dip gated by ADX < 20 (range-only mean reversion)
rule: Bands as in Bollinger(20,2). ADX(14) Wilder: TR, +DM, -DM smoothed with RMA alpha=1/14; +DI=100*s(+DM)/s(TR); -DI likewise; DX=100*|+DI - -DI|/(+DI + -DI); ADX = RMA14 of DX. ENTER long when flat AND ADX < 20 AND close < lower band. EXIT when close >= mid (SMA20) OR ADX > 30 OR 15 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Band tags mean-revert in ranges and 'walk the band' in trends; the ADX gate is how retail is taught to separate the two, and the ETF Bollinger tests so far were ungated.
source: Bollinger (2001) ch.19 on indicator confirmation; Investopedia 'Bollinger Bands + ADX'; Babypips

name: Bollinger lower band + Stochastic cross-up (classic combo)
rule: Bands as in Bollinger(20,2). Stoch(14,3,3): fastK = 100*(close - LL14)/(HH14 - LL14) (LL/HH of low/high incl. bar i; 50 if HH==LL); slowK = SMA3(fastK); D = SMA3(slowK). ENTER long when close[i-1] < lower[i-1] (or close[i] < lower[i]) AND slowK[i] < 20 at some bar within i-3..i AND slowK[i-1] <= D[i-1] AND slowK[i] > D[i]. EXIT when close >= mid OR slowK > 80 OR 10 bars held. Long only.
rationale: The Bollinger + Stochastic pairing is a top-3 retail 'combo' (Bollinger + RSI already tested here): the stochastic cross supplies the timing that a bare band tag lacks.
source: Investopedia 'Bollinger Bands and Stochastics'; Lane (1984) stochastics; Bollinger (2001)

name: Stochastic pop (Bernstein/Steckler): buy %K crossing above 80
rule: Stoch(14,3,3): fastK = 100*(close - LL14)/(HH14 - LL14) (LL/HH of low/high incl. bar i; 50 if HH==LL); slowK = SMA3(fastK); D = SMA3(slowK). ADX(14) Wilder: TR, +DM, -DM smoothed with RMA alpha=1/14; +DI=100*s(+DM)/s(TR); -DI likewise; DX=100*|+DI - -DI|/(+DI + -DI); ADX = RMA14 of DX. ENTER long when slowK[i-1] <= 80 AND slowK[i] > 80 AND ADX < 20 (Steckler's low-ADX filter). EXIT when slowK < 70. Long only.
rationale: Inverts the textbook: an overbought stochastic in a non-trending market signals the start of a thrust, not its end. Steckler's version adds ADX < 20 so the pop comes out of a base.
source: Jake Bernstein, The Compleat Day Trader (1995) 'stochastic pop'; David Steckler, 'Stochastics Pop', TASC Aug 2000

name: Stochastic bullish divergence (price lower low, %K higher low)
rule: Stoch(14,3,3): fastK = 100*(close - LL14)/(HH14 - LL14) (LL/HH of low/high incl. bar i; 50 if HH==LL); slowK = SMA3(fastK); D = SMA3(slowK). fractal low at bar k: low[k] < low[k-1], low[k-2], low[k+1], low[k+2], known at bar k+2; fractal high symmetric. Keep the last two confirmed fractal lows L1 (older) and L2 (newer) with 10 <= gap <= 40 bars. Divergence when low[L2] < low[L1] AND slowK[L2] > slowK[L1] AND slowK[L1] < 20. ENTER long on the first bar i with L2+2 <= i <= L2+12 where slowK[i-1] <= D[i-1] AND slowK[i] > D[i] (Lane %K/%D buy cross); if none by L2+12 the setup expires. EXIT when slowK > 80 OR close < low[L2] OR 15 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Divergence is the signal Lane himself said the stochastic was for; the RSI version has been tested here, the stochastic version (the one most chart tutorials draw) has not.
source: George Lane, 'Lane's Stochastics', TASC May/June 1984; Murphy (1999) ch.10

name: Ichimoku full five-line confirmation (price, TK, cloud, future cloud, Chikou)
rule: Ichimoku(t,k,s,shift): Tenkan=(HH_t+LL_t)/2, Kijun=(HH_k+LL_k)/2, SenkouA=(Tenkan+Kijun)/2, SenkouB=(HH_s+LL_s)/2; the cloud UNDER bar i uses SenkouA/B computed at bar i-shift (cloudTop=max, cloudBot=min) with (9,26,52,26). ENTER long when close > cloudTop AND Tenkan > Kijun AND SenkouA(i) > SenkouB(i) (future cloud bullish) AND close[i] > close[i-26] (Chikou above price). EXIT when close < Kijun OR close < cloudBot. Long only.
rationale: The earlier Ichimoku test used only a cloud breakout + TK cross; purists insist the signal is invalid without the future-cloud and Chikou confirmations, and that is the version sold in every Ichimoku course.
source: Nicole Elliott, Ichimoku Charts (Harriman House 2007); Goichi Hosoda (1969)

name: Ichimoku Kijun-sen bounce in an uptrend
rule: Ichimoku(t,k,s,shift): Tenkan=(HH_t+LL_t)/2, Kijun=(HH_k+LL_k)/2, SenkouA=(Tenkan+Kijun)/2, SenkouB=(HH_s+LL_s)/2; the cloud UNDER bar i uses SenkouA/B computed at bar i-shift (cloudTop=max, cloudBot=min) (9,26,52,26). Uptrend = close > cloudTop AND Tenkan > Kijun. ENTER long when flat AND uptrend AND min(low over i-2..i) <= Kijun*1.005 AND close[i] > Kijun AND close[i] > close[i-1]. EXIT when close < Kijun*0.99 OR close < cloudBot OR 20 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Kijun is taught as the equilibrium line; buying the first bounce off it in an established trend is the Ichimoku pullback entry, distinct from the breakout entry already tested.
source: Elliott (2007) ch.4 'Kijun-sen'; Manesh Patel, Trading with Ichimoku Clouds (Wiley 2010)

name: Supertrend(10,3) flip filtered by the 200 EMA
rule: Supertrend(n,m): hl2 +/- m*ATR(n) (ctx.atr), standard final-band carry-forward rule; bullish when close > final lower band after a flip, bearish when close < final upper band (10,3). ENTER long when ST flips to bullish on bar i AND close > ctx.ema('close',200). EXIT when ST flips bearish. Long only.
rationale: The most common Supertrend tweak: take flips only in the direction of the 200 EMA. Supertrend alone was tested on stocks; the filter is the open question.
source: TradingView 'Supertrend + EMA 200' scripts; retail trading education (e.g. Trade Pro, Rayner Teo)

name: Supertrend computed on Heikin Ashi candles
rule: Heikin Ashi: haClose=(o+h+l+c)/4; haOpen=(prevHaOpen+prevHaClose)/2 (bar 0: (o+c)/2); haHigh=max(h,haOpen,haClose); haLow=min(l,haOpen,haClose). Compute Supertrend(10,3) on the HA series (ATR from HA high/low/close with Wilder smoothing, hl2 from HA high/low). ENTER long when haClose > the ST line (bullish). EXIT on the bearish flip. Long only.
rationale: Smoothing the input with Heikin Ashi is how retail removes Supertrend whipsaws; it delays entries by design, so the net effect after crypto costs is unknown.
source: 'Heikin Ashi Supertrend' TradingView scripts and YouTube strategy videos (2020-2022); Valcu (2004) Heikin Ashi

name: Turtle 20/10 Donchian breakout gated by ADX >= 25
rule: ADX(14) Wilder: TR, +DM, -DM smoothed with RMA alpha=1/14; +DI=100*s(+DM)/s(TR); -DI likewise; DX=100*|+DI - -DI|/(+DI + -DI); ADX = RMA14 of DX. ENTER long when close > ctx.donchian(20, i-1).upper AND ADX >= 25 AND +DI > -DI. EXIT when close < ctx.donchian(10, i-1).lower. Long only.
rationale: The plain 20/10 breakout is already tested; the ADX gate is the most prescribed fix for breakout false starts, so it is the 'does the fix work' question retail asks.
source: Curtis Faith, Way of the Turtle (2007) for 20/10; Wilder (1978) ADX; ADX-filtered breakout tutorials (Investopedia, Babypips)

name: Keltner channel pullback buy in an uptrend (Raschke-style)
rule: mid=ctx.ema('close',20); lower = mid - 2*ctx.atr(10). ENTER long when flat AND close < lower AND close > ctx.ema('close',200). EXIT when close >= mid OR close < EMA200 OR 10 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Keltner bands are ATR-scaled, so a close below the lower band in an uptrend is a measured overshoot rather than a percentage one; the stock-only Keltner test here was a breakout, not the pullback.
source: Chester Keltner (1960); Linda Raschke's Keltner channel settings (20 EMA, 2x ATR10), LBR Group

name: ADX turning up from below 20 with +DI leading (Wilder trend-start)
rule: ADX(14) Wilder: TR, +DM, -DM smoothed with RMA alpha=1/14; +DI=100*s(+DM)/s(TR); -DI likewise; DX=100*|+DI - -DI|/(+DI + -DI); ADX = RMA14 of DX. ENTER long when flat AND min(ADX over i-5..i-1) < 20 AND ADX[i] > ADX[i-1] > ADX[i-2] AND +DI > -DI. EXIT when -DI > +DI. Long only.
rationale: Wilder's stated use of ADX: a rise out of the sub-20 zone marks a trend beginning, which is earlier than the ADX > 25 confirmation used by the DI-cross test already in the ledger.
source: Wilder (1978) pp.47-52; Chuck LeBeau & David Lucas, Technical Traders Guide to Computer Analysis of the Futures Market (1992) on ADX turning points

name: DI-cross trend with ADX peak exit (exhaustion above 40)
rule: ADX(14) Wilder: TR, +DM, -DM smoothed with RMA alpha=1/14; +DI=100*s(+DM)/s(TR); -DI likewise; DX=100*|+DI - -DI|/(+DI + -DI); ADX = RMA14 of DX. ENTER long when +DI > -DI AND ADX > 25. EXIT when (ADX > 40 AND ADX[i] < ADX[i-1]) OR -DI > +DI. After a peak exit, do not re-enter until ADX < 25 again. Long only.
rationale: Same entry as the tested DI cross, different exit: an ADX rollover above 40 is the textbook trend-exhaustion signal; whether it beats waiting for the DI cross is the retail 'when to take profit' question.
source: Wilder (1978); Murphy (1999) ch.10 'ADX line turning down from above 40'

name: Year-to-date anchored VWAP trend filter (Shannon)

params.anchor: first bar of each UTC calendar year

rule: AVWAP = sum(typical*volume)/sum(volume) since the first bar of the current UTC year, typical=(h+l+c)/3, reset at the first bar of each new year. ENTER long when close > AVWAP. EXIT when close < AVWAP*0.99. Long only.
rationale: The YTD anchored VWAP is the average price every holder who bought this year paid; being above it means the average buyer is in profit, which Shannon argues is the strongest trend-health reading retail has access to.
source: Brian Shannon, Maximum Trading Gains with Anchored VWAP (2021)

name: Anchored VWAP from the 52-week high: reclaim buy
rule: Anchor = index of the highest high over bars i-251..i (re-anchor whenever a new 252-bar high prints). AVWAP from the anchor bar. ENTER long when flat AND close[i-1] < AVWAP[i-1] AND close[i] > AVWAP[i] (first reclaim). AVWAP[i-1] and AVWAP[i] both use the anchor in effect at bar i (on the anchor bar AVWAP = that bar's typical price). If the old high rolls out of the 252-bar window the anchor moves to the new window max (no exit). EXIT when close < AVWAP*0.98 OR high[i] > max(high over i-251..i-1) (a fresh 52-week high = target reached). Long only.
rationale: Shannon's reclaim rule: once price gets back above the average cost of everyone who bought since the high, overhead supply is absorbed and the correction is over.
source: Shannon (2021) ch.6 'Anchoring to significant highs'

name: Monthly anchored VWAP with a 0.3% band (hourly crypto)

params.anchor: first bar of each UTC calendar month

rule: AVWAP since the first 1h bar of the current UTC month, typical=(h+l+c)/3. ENTER long when close > AVWAP*1.003. EXIT when close < AVWAP*0.997. Long only.
rationale: Monthly AVWAP is a standard on crypto Twitter as the 'institutional cost basis' for the month; the band avoids ping-pong around the line.
source: Shannon (2021); TradingView 'Anchored VWAP' monthly anchor default; crypto VWAP tutorials

name: Heikin Ashi strong candles (no lower wick) continuation (Valcu)
rule: Heikin Ashi: haClose=(o+h+l+c)/4; haOpen=(prevHaOpen+prevHaClose)/2 (bar 0: (o+c)/2); haHigh=max(h,haOpen,haClose); haLow=min(l,haOpen,haClose). strong(i) = haClose > haOpen AND haLow >= haOpen*(1-0.0005). ENTER long when strong(i) AND strong(i-1). EXIT when haClose < haOpen (first red HA candle). Long only.
rationale: Valcu's original HA paper: candles with no lower shadow mark a strong trend; the already-tested colour flip ignores the wick, which is the part HA traders actually watch.
source: Dan Valcu, 'Using the Heikin-Ashi Technique', TASC Feb 2004

name: Camarilla L3 bounce with L4 stop (Ochoa)
rule: Prior UTC day H,L,C from the 1h bars (day = floor(time/86400)). L3 = C - (H-L)*1.1/4; L4 = C - (H-L)*1.1/2; P=(H+L+C)/3. ENTER long when flat AND low[i] <= L3 AND close[i] > L3. EXIT when close < L4 OR close >= P OR the bar hour == 23 (flat at day end). Long only. Entries only on bars with UTC hour < 23. Exit conditions are checked from the bar after entry.
rationale: Camarilla levels are the most-searched intraday pivot variant; the L3 bounce / L4 stop is its canonical mean-reversion play, and it has no test here.
source: Frank Ochoa, Secrets of a Pivot Boss (2010) ch.7; Nick Stott's Camarilla equation (1989)

name: Weekly floor pivot as a trend line (above P long, below S1 flat)
rule: W = ctx.resample(bars,'1w'); from the last COMPLETE week: P=(H+L+C)/3, S1=2P-H. ENTER long when close > P. EXIT when close < S1. Long only.
rationale: Weekly pivots are the swing trader's version of the daily floor pivot; holding above P with an S1 stop is how they are taught as a regime line rather than a bounce level.
source: Floor-trader pivots (Murphy 1999 appendix); Ochoa (2010) ch.9 'weekly pivots'

name: Narrow CPR breakout (Ochoa central pivot range)
rule: Prior UTC day H,L,C. P=(H+L+C)/3, BC=(H+L)/2, TC=2P-BC, width=|TC-BC|/P. narrow = prior-day width < 0.5 * mean of the 10 complete-day widths ending with the prior day (inclusive); skip until 10 complete days exist. ENTER long when narrow AND the bar's UTC hour <= 12 AND close > prior-day H. EXIT when close < P OR bar hour == 23. Long only.
rationale: A narrow CPR is Ochoa's volatility-contraction tell for a trending day; trading the prior-day-high break on such days is the setup his book is best known for.
source: Ochoa (2010) ch.3 'The Central Pivot Range' and 'narrow CPR'

name: Traders Dynamic Index (TDI) fast/slow cross above 50
rule: r=ctx.rsi(13). fast = SMA2(r), slow = SMA7(r), base = SMA34(r) (ctx.rolling). ENTER long when fast[i-1] <= slow[i-1] AND fast[i] > slow[i] AND fast > 50 AND slow > base. EXIT when fast < slow. Long only.
rationale: TDI is the most-downloaded indicator on forex forums; it wraps RSI in its own moving averages and volatility band so one panel gives trend, momentum and volatility. Never tested formally here.
source: Dean Malone, 'Traders Dynamic Index' (2006, ForexFactory); TradingView 'TDI' scripts

name: ConnorsRSI < 10 above the 200-day SMA
rule: streak = signed count of consecutive up/down closes; CRSI = (RSI(3) of close + RSI(2) of streak + PercentRank over the last 100 bars of today's 1-day return)/3, PercentRank = share of prior 100 returns below today's *100. ENTER long when CRSI < 10 AND close > ctx.sma('close',200). EXIT when CRSI > 70. Long only.
rationale: ConnorsRSI blends three mean-reversion inputs that each work weakly (RSI(2), cumRSI(2), Double 7 are all in the ledger); the composite is Connors' own flagship and the one his courses sell.
source: Larry Connors & Cesar Alvarez, 'An Introduction to ConnorsRSI' (Connors Research 2012)

name: Elder-Ray: bear power rising from below with a rising EMA
rule: e=ctx.ema('close',13); bull = high - e; bear = low - e. ENTER long when e[i] > e[i-1] AND bear[i] < 0 AND bear[i] > bear[i-1]. EXIT when bull < 0 OR e[i] < e[i-1] OR 20 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Elder-Ray buys when the bears are losing power inside a rising trend; it is the entry rule from Elder's book that has not been covered by the Impulse-system test.
source: Alexander Elder, Trading for a Living (1993), ch.24 'Elder-ray'

name: TradingView Technical Rating 'Strong Buy'
rule: Votes per TradingView docs. MA group (each +1 if close > MA, -1 if below): SMA10,20,30,50,100,200; EMA10,20,30,50,100,200; VWMA20 (sum(c*v)/sum(v)); Hull MA9 (WMA(2*WMA(n/2)-WMA(n)), sqrt n); Ichimoku(9,26,52): +1 if Tenkan>Kijun AND close>cloudTop(i-26) AND SenkouA(i)>SenkouB(i), -1 if all reversed, else 0. Oscillator group: RSI14 (+1 if <30 and rising, -1 if >70 and falling); Stoch(14,3,3) (+1 if K<20 and K>D, -1 if K>80 and K<D); CCI20 (+1 if <-100 and rising, -1 if >100 and falling); ADX14 (+1 if ADX>20 and +DI>-DI, -1 if ADX>20 and -DI>+DI); AO (+1 saucer-up or cross above 0, -1 mirror); Momentum10 (+1 if close-close[i-10] rising); MACD(12,26,9) (+1 line>signal); StochRSI(3,3,14,14) (+1 K<20 and K>D, -1 K>80 and K<D); Williams %R14 (+1 < -80 and rising, -1 > -20 and falling); Bull/Bear Power 13 (+1 if bear<0 rising and EMA13 rising, -1 mirror); Ultimate Osc(7,14,28) (+1 >70, -1 <30). Zero vote otherwise. rating = (mean(MA votes) + mean(osc votes))/2. ENTER long when rating > 0.5 (Strong Buy). EXIT when rating < 0.1 (no longer Buy). Long only. Precise definitions: 'rising'/'falling' = value[i] > / < value[i-1]. HMA9 = WMA(2*WMA(close,4) - WMA(close,9), 3). CCI20 = (tp - SMA20(tp))/(0.015*meanAbsDev20(tp)), tp=(h+l+c)/3. AO = SMA5(hl2)-SMA34(hl2); +1 if (AO[i-1] <= 0 < AO[i]) OR (AO[i] > 0 AND AO[i-2] > AO[i-1] AND AO[i] > AO[i-1]); -1 mirror. Momentum10 m = close - close[i-10]: +1 if m rising, -1 if falling. MACD: +1 line > signal, -1 line < signal. StochRSI: K = SMA3 of 100*(RSI14 - min14(RSI14))/(max14 - min14) (50 if max==min), D = SMA3(K). Ultimate Osc(7,14,28) standard Williams weights 4/2/1. Each group mean is over the indicators that have a value; rating undefined (flat) until all MA-group inputs exist (needs 200 bars).
rationale: The 'Strong Buy' gauge on every TradingView symbol page is probably the most-viewed technical signal in the world; nobody has published whether following it beats holding.
source: TradingView Help Center, 'Technical Ratings' (https://www.tradingview.com/support/solutions/43000614331/)

name: Vegas Tunnel (EMA 144/169) with EMA 12 trigger
rule: t1=ctx.ema('close',144), t2=ctx.ema('close',169), top=max(t1,t2), bot=min(t1,t2), f=ctx.ema('close',12). ENTER long when close > top AND f[i-1] <= top[i-1] AND f[i] > top[i]. EXIT when close < bot. Long only.
rationale: The Vegas tunnel is a forex-forum classic adapted wholesale to crypto hourly charts; the 144/169 band is treated as dynamic support and the fast EMA re-cross as the entry.
source: 'Vegas' (pseudonymous), 'Vegas Tunnel Method', ForexFactory 2004; widely re-posted on TradingView for crypto 1h

name: Ripster EMA clouds (5/12 over 34/50) stacked long
rule: e5,e12,e34,e50 = ctx.ema('close',n). ENTER long when e5 > e12 AND e34 > e50 AND min(e5,e12) > max(e34,e50) AND close > e34. EXIT when close < min(e34,e50). Long only.
rationale: Ripster's EMA clouds are the most-shared discretionary trend tool on finance Twitter since 2020; the stacked-cloud rule is its mechanical core and has not been tested anywhere here.
source: Ripster47, 'Ripster EMA Clouds' TradingView script (2020) and Twitter threads

name: Alt/BTC ratio above its 50-day SMA (alts that beat Bitcoin)
rule: rank() daily. For each alt (not BTCUSDT) with >= 50 bars: ratio = close_alt/close_BTC; hold if ratio > SMA50(ratio) AND close_BTC > SMA50(close_BTC). Weights: equal 1/N across holders (N = count of qualifying alts). If N == 0: weight 1 in BTCUSDT if close_BTC > SMA50 else all cash. Long only.
rationale: Retail judges alts on their BTC pair ('is it outperforming BTC?'); a ratio above its 50-day average is the simplest coding of that, and only in a BTC uptrend because alts bleed in BTC downtrends.
source: TradingView ALT/BTC pair convention; Binance Academy 'altcoin season'; CryptoCred 'alt/BTC charts' (2019)

name: O'Neil follow-through day market buy
rule: Correction = close < 0.90 * max(high over i-59..i). Rally attempt day 1 = first close > close[i-1] while in correction; rallyLow = min(low over the 20 bars ending at day 1). Day count increments each bar (correction need not persist after day 1); if close < rallyLow the attempt resets; if day 7 passes without an FTD the attempt expires and a new one needs a new day-1 while in correction. FTD = day 4..7 of the attempt with close/close[i-1]-1 >= 0.0125 AND volume > volume[i-1]. ENTER long on the FTD close. EXIT when close < rallyLow OR 60 bars held. Long only. SPY proxied by QQQ/DIA. proxyFor goes in meta.proxyFor; QQQ and DIA are in assets.
rationale: O'Neil's FTD is the IBD 'market in confirmed uptrend' signal: a strong day on rising volume several days into a rally attempt indicates institutions, not shorts, are buying. Distribution days (the sell side) are tested; the buy side is not.
source: William O'Neil, How to Make Money in Stocks (4th ed. 2009), ch.7 'follow-through day'

name: Grid-bot exposure around the 50-day SMA (Pionex/3Commas style)
rule: rank() daily. For each coin with >= 50 bars: c = SMA50(close); g = clamp(0.5 + (c - close)/(0.20*c), 0, 1) (fully long 10% below the centre, flat 10% above, linear between = a 20-level grid). weight = g / N where N = coins with >= 50 bars. Long only.
rationale: Grid bots are the most-used retail crypto automation; this is the equal-weight, fractional-exposure equivalent of a symmetric grid centred on a moving average, which answers 'do grid bots beat holding' net of costs.
source: Pionex 'Grid Trading Bot' docs; 3Commas GRID bot; Binance Academy 'What is grid trading'

name: Bullish Gartley harmonic (0.618 B, 0.786 D) on fractal pivots
rule: fractal low at bar k: low[k] < low[k-1], low[k-2], low[k+1], low[k+2], known at bar k+2; fractal high symmetric. Pivots form a zigzag: a new confirmed pivot of the same type as the last one replaces it only if more extreme (lower low / higher high), else it is ignored. Keep the last 5 alternating pivots X(low),A(high),B(low),C(high),D(low) spanning <= 60 bars. XA=A-X; AB=A-B; BC=C-B; CD=C-D. Valid when |AB/XA - 0.618| <= 0.05 AND 0.382 <= BC/AB <= 0.886 AND |(A-D)/XA - 0.786| <= 0.05 AND D > X. ENTER long on the bar D is confirmed if close > D. EXIT when close >= D + 0.618*(A-D) OR close < X OR 30 bars held. Long only. Universe US_STOCKS_WIDE (171 names): on the 40-name set the pattern fires too rarely (< 30 trades).
rationale: Harmonics are a huge retail niche; the Gartley is its founding pattern and a fixed-ratio pullback-in-trend test with explicit stop and target, which makes it falsifiable.
source: H.M. Gartley, Profits in the Stock Market (1935), p.222; Scott Carney, The Harmonic Trader (1999)

name: The Strat 2-1-2 bullish reversal
rule: Bar types vs the previous bar: 1 = inside (high <= high[-1] AND low >= low[-1]); 2u = high > high[-1] AND low >= low[-1]; 2d = low < low[-1] AND high <= high[-1]; 3 = outside. ENTER long when type(i-2) == 2d AND type(i-1) == 1 AND type(i) == 2u AND close[i] > open[i]. EXIT when close < low[i-1] (the inside bar's low) OR type == 2d OR 5 bars held. Long only.
rationale: The Strat is one of the largest retail price-action communities; the 2-1-2 reversal is its bread-and-butter entry and is fully mechanical, so it can actually be scored.
source: Rob Smith, 'The Strat' (2016 onward, YouTube/Twitter); community wiki 'Strat bar types'

name: Al Brooks H2 second-entry buy above the 20 EMA
rule: e=ctx.ema('close',20). trend = close > e on each of the last 10 bars. Pullback leg starts when high[i] < high[i-1]. H1 = first bar after that with high > high[i-1]. If after H1 another bar prints high < high[i-1], H2 = the next bar with high > high[i-1]. ENTER long on the H2 bar close if trend AND close > e. The H1/H2 count resets when any close < e, after an H2 bar (entered or not), and after 20 bars without an H2; a new pullback leg can then start. The pullback low is tracked from the leg start to the H2 bar. stop = min(low) over the whole pullback. EXIT when close < stop OR close >= entry + 2*(entry - stop) OR 15 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Brooks teaches that the second attempt to resume a trend (H2) traps the early shorts and is the highest-probability with-trend entry; it is widely imitated and never formalised in a backtest here.
source: Al Brooks, Trading Price Action Trends (Wiley 2012), ch.3 'H1 and H2'

name: Hikkake bullish (failed inside-bar breakdown)
rule: inside(i-1): high[i-1] <= high[i-2] AND low[i-1] >= low[i-2]. Hikkake bar i: low[i] < low[i-1] AND high[i] <= high[i-1]. ENTER long within the next 3 bars on the first close > high[i-1] (the inside bar's high). EXIT when close < low[i] (hikkake bar low) OR 10 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Chesler's pattern trades the trap: breakout traders short the inside-bar breakdown and are forced to cover when price reverses through the inside bar's high.
source: Daniel L. Chesler, 'Trading False Moves with the Hikkake Pattern', Active Trader April 2004; TASC

name: Ascending triangle breakout (Bulkowski)
rule: Over bars i-40..i-1 (bar i excluded): R = max high. Touches = bars with high >= R*0.99, counted only if >= 5 bars from the previous touch; need >= 3. fractal low at bar k: low[k] < low[k-1], low[k-2], low[k+1], low[k+2], known at bar k+2; fractal high symmetric; each gap between consecutive touches must contain at least one fractal low (confirmed by bar i-1), and the lowest fractal low per gap must be strictly higher than in the previous gap. No close > R inside the window before bar i. ENTER long when close[i] > R and the pattern is valid. target = R + (R - lowest fractal low in the pattern). EXIT when close >= target OR close < last fractal low OR 30 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Bulkowski ranks the ascending triangle among the better-performing continuation patterns; it is mechanically definable (flat top, rising lows) and a top retail search term.
source: Thomas Bulkowski, Encyclopedia of Chart Patterns (2nd ed. 2005), ch.46

name: Tweezer bottom at a 20-day low
rule: ENTER long when close[i-1] < open[i-1] AND close[i] > open[i] AND |low[i]-low[i-1]|/low[i] <= 0.001 AND min(low[i],low[i-1]) <= min(low over i-20..i-2). EXIT when close < min(low[i],low[i-1]) OR 10 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Two matching lows after a decline show sellers were rejected at the same price twice; Nison lists it as a reversal signal and crypto's precise 24/7 lows make the equality test meaningful.
source: Steve Nison, Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques (2nd ed. 2001), ch.6 'Tweezers'

name: Piercing line after a 5-day decline
rule: ENTER long when close[i-1] < open[i-1] AND close[i-6] > close[i-1] AND open[i] < low[i-1] AND close[i] > (open[i-1]+close[i-1])/2 AND close[i] < open[i-1]. EXIT when close < low[i] OR 10 bars held. Long only.
rationale: The piercing line needs a real gap down that reverses, which daily stocks produce; it is the two-candle reversal most tutorials list after the engulfing (already tested).
source: Nison (2001) ch.4 'Piercing pattern'; Bulkowski, Encyclopedia of Candlestick Charts (2008)

name: VSA stopping volume (ultra-high volume down bar closing in the upper half)
rule: ENTER long when close[i] < close[i-1] AND volume[i] > 2*ctx.sma('volume',20) AND (close[i]-low[i])/(high[i]-low[i]) >= 0.5 AND low[i] <= min(low over i-20..i-1). EXIT when close < low[i] OR 10 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Volume Spread Analysis reads a huge-volume down bar that closes off its low as professionals absorbing supply; it is the VSA setup retail most often asks to see tested.
source: Tom Williams, Master the Markets (TradeGuider 2000), 'stopping volume'; Richard Wyckoff's selling climax

name: OBV above its 20-day average with price above the 50-day SMA (Granville)
rule: OBV: cumulative +volume on up closes, -volume on down closes (0 on unchanged). ENTER long when OBV > SMA20(OBV) AND close > ctx.sma('close',50). EXIT when OBV < SMA20(OBV). Long only.
rationale: Granville's thesis is that volume leads price; requiring OBV to be above its own trend while price is above its 50-day filters trends that lack participation. OBV divergence is tested, the trend-confirmation use is not.
source: Joseph Granville, Granville's New Key to Stock Market Profits (1963)

name: Percent envelope (SMA20, 10%) lower-band buy
rule: m=ctx.sma('close',20). ENTER long when close < m*0.90. EXIT when close >= m. Long only.
rationale: Fixed-percentage envelopes predate Bollinger Bands and are the TradingView 'Envelope' default (20, 10%); they do not shrink in quiet markets, so the signal fires only on genuine 10% dislocations.
source: Murphy (1999) ch.9 'Percentage envelopes'; TradingView built-in 'Envelope' (length 20, 10%)

name: Linear regression channel: buy the -2 sigma line in a rising channel
rule: Fit close = a + b*k by least squares over bars i-99..i (k = 0..99); fitEnd = a + 99b; s = std of residuals. ENTER long when flat AND b > 0 AND close < fitEnd - 2s. EXIT when close >= fitEnd OR b <= 0 OR 20 bars held. Long only.
rationale: The TradingView Linear Regression Channel is drawn on millions of charts; buying the lower band of an up-sloping channel is its default play and is a different estimator from Bollinger's SMA-centred bands.
source: Gilbert Raff, 'Trading the Regression Channel' (1996); TradingView 'Linear Regression Channel' built-in

name: Tillson T3(20) trend line
rule: T3 per Tillson: six chained EMAs of length 20 (custom EMA: alpha=2/(n+1), seeded with the first available value) e1..e6; c1=-v^3, c2=3v^2+3v^3, c3=-6v^2-3v-3v^3, c4=1+3v+v^3+3v^2 with v=0.7; T3=c1*e6+c2*e5+c3*e4+c4*e3. ENTER long when close > T3 AND T3[i] > T3[i-1]. EXIT when close < T3. Long only.
rationale: T3 is a low-lag smoother that is a TradingView staple; a rising T3 with price above it is the stock 'smooth trend' rule and has not been run, unlike Hull/KAMA/VIDYA which have.
source: Tim Tillson, 'Smoothing Techniques for More Accurate Signals', TASC Jan 1998

name: ALMA 9/50 crossover
rule: ALMA(n): weights w_k = exp(-(k - m)^2/(2 s^2)) for k=0..n-1, m = offset*(n-1), s = n/sigma, normalised; value = sum(w_k * close[i-(n-1)+k]). fast=ALMA(9), slow=ALMA(50). ENTER long when fast crosses above slow. EXIT when fast crosses below slow. Long only.
rationale: ALMA is a Gaussian-weighted average with less lag than an EMA at the same length; its crossover is a popular TradingView replacement for the EMA cross (which is tested here).
source: Arnaud Legoux & Dimitrios Kouzis-Loukas, 'Arnaud Legoux Moving Average' (2009); TradingView built-in ALMA

name: Landry three-bar pullback in a rising 50-day SMA
rule: m=ctx.sma('close',50); trend = close > m AND m[i] > m[i-5]. Pullback = at least 3 consecutive bars with lower highs (high[k] < high[k-1]) ending at bar i-1. ENTER long when trend AND pullback AND close[i] > high[i-1]. stop = min(low) of the pullback bars. EXIT when close < stop OR close >= entry + 2*(entry - stop) OR 15 bars held. Long only.
rationale: Landry's pullback is the most-taught swing entry for US stocks: a trend, a brief orderly retreat of lower highs, and a buy on the first bar that takes out the prior high.
source: Dave Landry, Dave Landry on Swing Trading (M. Gordon 2000), ch.4 'Pullbacks'

name: 200-day EMA touch-and-hold in an established uptrend
rule: e=ctx.ema('close',200). ENTER long when flat AND close > e on each of the last 20 bars AND low[i] <= e*1.01 AND close[i] > e. EXIT when close < e*0.97 OR close >= entry*1.10 OR 40 bars held. Long only.
rationale: The '200 EMA bounce' is the first setup most YouTube trading courses teach; the EMA20 pullback is in the ledger, the 200-day touch is not.
source: Investopedia 'The 200-day moving average'; Rayner Teo 'The 200 EMA trading strategy'; Murphy (1999) ch.9

name: New York open range breakout on hourly crypto
rule: Each UTC day: range = max high / min low of the bars whose UTC hour is 13 or 14 (covers the 13:30/14:30 US cash open across DST). ENTER long when flat AND the bar hour is 15..18 AND close > rangeHigh. EXIT when close < rangeLow OR the bar hour == 20 (flat before the US close). One trade per day. Long only.
rationale: Crypto has traded increasingly in step with US equities; the US-open range breakout is the retail adaptation of Crabel's ORB to a 24/7 market, distinct from the UTC-midnight ORB already tested.
source: Toby Crabel, Day Trading with Short Term Price Patterns and Opening Range Breakout (1990); crypto 'NY session ORB' tutorials

name: Previous-day-high close-through continuation
rule: ENTER long when close[i] > high[i-1] AND close[i] > open[i]. Hold exactly 2 bars (holdBars: 2), then flat; re-enter on the next qualifying bar. Long only. Signals during the 2-bar hold are ignored; if the bar that completes the hold itself qualifies, stay long and restart the 2-bar count.
rationale: Breaking and holding above yesterday's high is the simplest ICT/price-action continuation rule and retail asks about it constantly; the sweep (fade) version is tested, the close-through is not.
source: ICT 'previous day high' concept; Larry Williams, Long-Term Secrets to Short-Term Trading (1999) on taking out the prior day's high

name: Previous-week-high breakout with previous-week-low exit
rule: W = ctx.resample(bars,'1w'); PWH, PWL = high/low of the last COMPLETE week. ENTER long when close > PWH. EXIT when close < PWL. Long only.
rationale: The weekly-range breakout is the swing version of the prior-day rule: holding above last week's high with last week's low as the line in the sand.
source: ICT / price-action 'PWH/PWL' convention; Murphy (1999) on weekly ranges

name: Donchian 20 breakout with a 1.618 Fibonacci extension target
rule: ENTER long when close > ctx.donchian(20, i-1).upper. swingLow = min(low over i-20..i-1); target = swingLow + 1.618*(close - swingLow); stop = swingLow. EXIT when close >= target OR close < stop OR 60 bars held. Long only. target and stop are fixed at entry.
rationale: Retail breakout traders almost universally set targets at the 1.618 extension; the ledger's Donchian tests all use channel exits, so this isolates whether the Fib target helps or hurts.
source: Robert Fischer, Fibonacci Applications and Strategies for Traders (Wiley 1993); TradingView 'Fib Extension' tool defaults

name: Awesome Oscillator twin peaks (Bill Williams)
rule: AO = SMA5(hl2) - SMA34(hl2). Trough at bar k: AO[k] < AO[k-1] AND AO[k] < AO[k+1], known at k+1. Keep the last two troughs T1 (older), T2 (newer) with AO < 0 at both and AO < 0 on every bar between them. ENTER long on the bar T2 is confirmed if AO[T2] > AO[T1] AND AO[i] < 0. EXIT when (AO > 0 AND AO[i] < AO[i-1]) OR AO < AO[T2] OR 20 bars held. Long only.
rationale: The third of Williams' three AO signals (saucer and zero-cross are tested); a higher trough below zero is his momentum-divergence buy.
source: Bill Williams, Trading Chaos (Wiley 1995), ch.8 'Awesome Oscillator'
